qt: to the Commission Jorge Buxadé Villalba (ECR) Subject:

According to the European Parliament study on ‘Cohesion policy in the outermost regions’ published in January 20241, the Canary Islands is the region that has experienced the sharpest decline in per capita GDP since 2001, dropping more than 20 %. According to the study, in 2000, it was the outermost region whose per capita GDP was closest to the EU average (97 %). Since its ‘staggering decline’, it has been overtaken by Martinique, Madeira, the Azores and Guadeloupe. In view of this study, I would ask the following questions: 1.

The Commission’s regional GDP data show that the fall in per capita GDP in the Canary Islands has been directly affected by the influx of 211 000 new residents into the region, which accounts for 40 % of the population growth, according to the data from the Government of the Canary Islands. Can the Commission explain where the other 60 % comes from?
Why has the Canary Islands received less cohesion funding per person than all of the other outermost regions, for both the 2014-2020 and 2021-2027 periods?
The Canary Islands were allocated EUR 402 million from the European Social Fund for the period 2014-2020. Why has only 35 % of this been used?
at: (English version) to the Commission Jorge Buxadé Villalba (ECR) (15 February 2024) Subject: Failed policies ruining the Canary Islands According to the European Parliament study on ‘Cohesion policy in the outermost regions’ published in January 2024 (1), the Canary Islands is the region that has experienced the sharpest decline in per capita GDP since 2001, dropping more than 20%. According to the study, in 2000, it was the outermost region whose per capita GDP was closest to the EU average (97%). Since its ‘staggering decline’, it has been overtaken by Martinique, Madeira, the Azores and Guadeloupe. In view of this study, I would ask the following questions: 1.

The Commission’s regional GDP data show that the fall in per capita GDP in the Canary Islands has been directly affected by the influx of 211 000 new residents into the region, which accounts for 40% of the population growth, according to the data from the Government of the Canary Islands. Can the Commission explain where the other 60% comes from?
Why has the Canary Islands received less cohesion funding per person than all of the other outermost regions, for both the 2014-2020 and 2021-2027 periods?
The Canary Islands were allocated EUR 402 million from the European Social Fund for the period 2014-2020. Why has only 35% of this been used?

(10 April 2024) The Commission takes note on the study commissioned by the Parliament and reiterates its commitment to the outermost regions, in line with Article 349 of the Treaty, as reflected in the 2022 Communication on the EU’s outermost regions (2). According to Eurostat, the Canary Islands’ gross domestic product (GPD) per capita as percentage of EU average decreased from 95% in 2000 to 68% in 2022 (an increase from 62% in 2020). Data show an increase of region’s population from 1 667 000 in 2000 to 2 189 000 in 2022, with 13.2% of growth attributed to natural change. The above-mentioned study states that 211 000 foreign residents caused 40% of population growth during the same period, based on regional government’s data. While movements from other regions of Spain to the Islands are the likely cause of the remaining increase, the Commission does not have data from the Spanish or regional governments. The methodology for the allocation of cohesion policy funds is described in Annex VII of Regulation 2013/1303 and Annex XXVI of Regulation 2021/1060 (3), whereby e.g. the additional specific allocation for outermost regions is calculated on the basis of a fixed amount per capita per region. As the most populated outermost region, the Canary Islands receive the highest allocation. The Open Data Platform (4) provides information on the implementation of the funds. The implementation rate 2014-2020 for the European Social Fund programme in the Islands was 69% on 31 December 2023.
